name: zttp
workload: 14-workload HTTP/1.1 parser microbenchmark suite (wrk/TFB/httparse/pico/llhttp/Chrome-nav/k8s-ingress/upload shapes) measuring messages/sec parsed via zttp's Zig core (Python binding) vs MagicStack/httptools, whose HttpRequestParser/HttpResponseParser are fulfilled through llhttp
claimed_speedup: beats httptools on 13 of 14 workloads, 1.04x-2.06x faster (e.g. 1.16x on wrk default GET, 2.06x on 16KB upload in MTU pieces, 1.14x on llhttp's own chunked-POST benchmark shape); 0.94x (slower) on one synthetic 16x-pipelined workload
compiler_and_flags: Zig ReleaseSafe build (safety checks on); CPython 3.14; httptools 0.8.0
hardware: "an Apple Silicon machine" (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: httptools is a thin C-parser binding while zttp's Zig core is sans-IO and event-based (Request/Data/EndOfMessage), which changes the integration API; zttp also ships HTTP/2 and experimental HTTP/3 support in the same package; explicitly marked experimental/not production-ready by the author
caveats: Hardware is described only as "an Apple Silicon machine", not an exact CPU model, and Zig compiler version is not stated, so this falls short of Tier A despite public benchmark code (benchmarks/http1.py) and a documented methodology; author states run-to-run spread is about 5%, comparable in size to several of the smaller reported wins; benchmarks measure parser throughput in isolation, not a full server
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "http parser" (basic query) surfaced Kludex/zttp; README performance section and https://zttp.marcelotryle.com/reference/performance/ opened directly

name: http.c3l
workload: pico's own benchmark request (request line + headers, no body) parsed in a tight loop on one pinned core, comparing http::parser's callback-driven and callback-free ("no cb") streaming request parser against vendored picohttpparser
claimed_speedup: callback-free parsing core is ~99 ns/req vs picohttpparser's ~112 ns/req (~13% faster, ~10.1M vs ~8.9M req/s); the full callback-driven parser is only at parity (~99% of pico's speed, same ~112 ns) because of per-token indirect-call overhead; against picohttpparser's scalar (non-SSE4.2) build the library's SSE2 path is ~1.5x faster
compiler_and_flags: c3c build at -O3; picohttpparser built -O3 -msse4.2; http::parser uses hand-written 16-byte SSE2/NEON vectors, no -march=native
hardware: "x86-64" only; exact CPU model not stated; author pins to one core with taskset
tradeoffs: http::parser is a sans-IO streaming push parser (callback per token, consume/re-present contract) vs picohttpparser's one-shot whole-buffer parse into caller arrays; the streaming design is what costs the ~10-15% callback overhead; written in C3, a young C-like systems language, not C or C++ directly (interoperable via C ABI)
caveats: Author's own README explicitly frames this as "indicative, not a verdict" given the differing parser shapes (streaming vs one-shot), and the headline "faster than picohttpparser" claim applies only to the callback-free core, not the usable callback-driven parser, which is merely at parity; no exact CPU model given, capping the tier below A despite otherwise thorough, public, reproducible methodology
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than picohttpparser" surfaced lsfratel/http.c3l:bench/README.md

name: ada-rs
workload: Rust port of the ada-url WHATWG URL parser benchmarked with black_box against the official C++ Ada 4.0.0 (via its Rust wrapper) and Servo's url crate, over a focused 9-URL corpus and the full ~891-case pinned WPT URL-parsing fixture
claimed_speedup: 7.4% faster than C++ Ada over the whole 9-URL corpus (1.041us vs 1.124us), 21.7% faster on the normalized-URL subset, tied at timer resolution on the complex subset; on the full WPT fixture: 0.6% faster overall, 3.2% faster on valid cases, 26.2% faster on invalid/error-path cases, 0.6% faster with a base URL, 0.4% slower without a base URL; also 37.5% faster than Servo's url crate on the 9-URL corpus
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.97.1, LLVM 22.1.8, opt-level=3, one codegen unit, fat LTO; C++ Ada via its official ada-url Rust wrapper v4.0.0
tradeoffs: forbids unsafe code (memory-safety goal) while claiming to match/beat a hand-optimized C++ SIMD parser; wins are modest (single-digit to ~20%) and one subset (no-base-URL WPT cases) is slightly slower; extremely new project, 0 stars, single author, not yet adopted anywhere
caveats: README itself calls these "local measurements, not universal performance claims" and says results should be remeasured per target CPU/toolchain; baseline (ada-url) is not one of the category's three named baselines (llhttp/http-parser/picohttpparser) but is the widely-used incumbent URL parser referenced in the orchestrator's own notes for this run
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "WHATWG URL parser" surfaced countradooku/ada-rs

name: lucid-url
workload: Google Benchmark comparison, official Ada v4 release-benchmark protocol (parse+href and can_parse, mean of five repetitions), run over Ada's pinned 100,025-URL dataset against a dependency-free Rust WHATWG URL parser with an Ada-compatible interface
claimed_speedup: Url parse+href: 85.41ns vs Ada's 108.54ns (1.27x faster); UrlAggregator parse+href: 59.70ns vs Ada's 57.26ns (0.96x, i.e. slower); can_parse: 12.95ns vs Ada's 11.25ns (0.87x, i.e. slower) -- mixed result, faster on only 1 of 3 measured operations
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.98.0, Apple Clang 21, ADA_USE_SIMDUTF=OFF, ADA_INCLUDE_URL_PATTERN=ON (matching Ada defaults); LTO settings matched between implementations
tradeoffs: no unsafe dependency on Ada itself (pure Rust, stdlib-only); the project's own README acknowledges Ada is faster on 2 of the 3 core parse/can_parse benchmarks and that 'parsing experiments did not show a dependable across-the-board gain'; native code footprint is 45% larger than Ada's
caveats: Only one of the three headline operations (owned Url parse+href) is actually faster than Ada; the other two (UrlAggregator parse+href, can_parse) are slower in the same run, per the project's own numbers -- this is a mixed, not a clean, win over the baseline
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "WHATWG URL parser" surfaced lucid-softworks/url

name: thhp (Totemo-Hayai HTTP Parser)
workload: cargo nightly bench (built-in #[bench], black_box) parsing a realistic full HTTP request and a short request, comparing thhp against picohttpparser-sys bindings and Rust's httparse crate
claimed_speedup: with SSE4.2 explicitly enabled: thhp 4421 MB/s vs picohttpparser 4393 MB/s (~0.6% faster) on the full request, and 1600 MB/s vs 1244 MB/s on the short request; with SSE4.2 only implicitly available: thhp drops to 3550 MB/s vs picohttpparser's 4594 MB/s (thhp is slower in this configuration)
compiler_and_flags: cargo +nightly bench; RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+sse4.2" for the explicit-SIMD run; no flag (implicit) for the second run
tradeoffs: requires Rust nightly (uses unstable #[bench]); results are inconsistent across the two reported runs, so any speed advantage over picohttpparser is not robust
caveats: No CPU model stated; the two reported benchmark runs disagree on whether thhp beats picohttpparser at all (marginal win with explicit SSE4.2, clear loss without it), so the 'faster than picohttpparser' framing in the README is only true in one of two shown configurations; last commit is from 2018
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "http parser" language:rust surfaced kei10in/thhp

name: ls-hpack (LiteSpeed HPACK)
workload: HTTP/2 HPACK header (de)compression, RFC 7541; no numeric benchmark published, only a qualitative claim from a downstream adopter
claimed_speedup: "faster than nghttp2's for our workloads" (no numbers given) -- stated in Bun's own build-dependency source comment explaining why Bun vendors ls-hpack instead of nghttp2's HPACK implementation
stars_or_usage: 56 stars; vendored into oven-sh/bun, and used in LiteSpeed's own web/QUIC server stack
tradeoffs: depends on xxhash at runtime; library itself ships no benchmark suite or numbers, so the speed claim is entirely third-party and unverified from ls-hpack's own repo
caveats: The claim has no numbers, methodology, hardware, or reproducible benchmark anywhere found -- it is a one-line justification comment in Bun's dependency-build script (scripts/build/deps/lshpack.ts), not a benchmark. Recorded as the single Tier D entry for this run because ls-hpack's own repo has no performance claims at all and notability comes from adoption (Bun, LiteSpeed's own servers) rather than stars
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than nghttp2" surfaced oven-sh/bun:scripts/build/deps/lshpack.ts (and several Bun forks with the same vendored comment)
